intro: Martial arts and combat sports do not live only in private schools. Armies taught them in training camps. Colleges built teams around them. Public schools in Japan, Okinawa and Illinois put them into the school day, often for a few weeks at a time. Each of these places changed the art to fit its own clock, its own goals and its own rules.

In this unit you will follow those changes with dates and documents. You will meet the 1917 camp boxing program, Yosh Uchida's judo team at San Jose State and Itosu Ankō's karate classes in Shuri. You will read the New York boxing laws of 1896, 1911 and 1920, the Lystedt Law of 2009 and Illinois's concussion laws. You will also see how Title IX and the Paralympic Games opened doors.

By the end, you will be able to explain who regulates a training room and a competition. You will compare a short school unit with a long teaching lineage. You will name the laws, agencies and governing bodies that answer when someone gets hurt, and say when each one began.
bigQuestion: When armies, schools and states take up a martial art, what do they keep, what do they leave out and who becomes responsible for safety?

timeline.t: The Queensberry Rules for gloved boxing are published in London
Kanō Jigorō founds the Kodokan judo school in Tokyo
Itosu Ankō begins teaching karate at Shuri Jinjō Elementary School
The War Department creates the Commission on Training Camp Activities
New York's Walker Law creates the State Athletic Commission
Executive Order 9066 leads to the forced removal of Japanese Americans
Yosh Uchida returns to coach judo at San Jose State
Judo debuts at the Tokyo Olympics
Title IX bans sex discrimination in federally funded school programs
The Amateur Sports Act sets one governing body for each Olympic sport
Washington passes the Lystedt Law on youth concussions
Illinois passes its first youth concussion law

in law, failing to use reasonable care in a way that causes harm

a private organization that ranks boxers and approves title fights

test.q: Which Gene Tunney title came from World War I service?
choices: the light heavyweight title of the American Expeditionary Forces
test.why: Tunney, a Marine, won the AEF light heavyweight title in 1919.

test.q: Who shaped many British combatives courses in World War II?
test.why: Fairbairn and Sykes, former Shanghai police officers, trained British commandos and agents from 1940.

test.q: In what year did the Marine Corps Martial Arts Program begin?
test.why: MCMAP began in 2001 with a belt system from tan to black.

test.q: What connects Yosh Uchida to Executive Order 9066?
choices: He was IOC president when it was signed.
He coached judo in Japan during the war.
His family was removed under it while he served in the U.S. Army.
test.why: Uchida's family was among the Japanese Americans removed in 1942, while he served in the Army.

test.q: Which statement about Olympic judo is accurate?
choices: It began at Tokyo in 1964, and women's judo became a medal event in 1992.
It began in 1904 at St. Louis.
It is run by the NFHS.
test.why: Judo debuted in 1964; women's judo was a demonstration in 1988 and a medal event in 1992.

test.q: What did Japan's Ministry of Education require starting in 2012?
choices: budo in the first two years of junior high PE
an end to all school judo
test.why: Japan's 2012 course of study required a martial art such as judo, kendo or sumo in junior high PE.

test.q: Why is Itosu Ankō's 1908 letter important to historians?
choices: It is an early written record of karate's purpose in schools.
It legalized boxing in New York.
test.why: Itosu's letter to education officials argued for karate in all Okinawan schools.

test.q: How does a koryu license differ from a judo dan rank?
choices: A dan rank is only for soldiers.
A koryu license is given after six weeks.
A koryu license records a line of teachers; dan ranks gave one school a clear ladder many could climb.
test.why: Koryu licenses pass authority through a lineage, while Kanō's 1883 dan ranks built an open ladder.

test.q: Which Illinois law protects school districts from many injury lawsuits?
choices: the Local Governmental and Governmental Employees Tort Immunity Act of 1965
test.why: The 1965 Tort Immunity Act shields public bodies, with exceptions for willful and wanton conduct.

test.q: What did New York's Walker Law of 1920 create?
choices: the New York State Athletic Commission
test.why: The Walker Law legalized boxing with decisions and created the lasting state commission.

test.q: Why did the WBC shorten title bouts to twelve rounds?
choices: Duk Koo Kim died after a fifteen-round title fight in 1982.
test.why: Kim died four days after his 1982 bout with Ray Mancini, and the WBC cut title fights to twelve rounds.

test.q: Which federal law requires commission supervision of every pro boxing bout?
choices: the Professional Boxing Safety Act of 1996
test.why: The 1996 law banned U.S. pro bouts without a state or tribal commission supervising.

test.q: What did the Lystedt Law of 2009 require for a young athlete with a suspected concussion?
choices: removal from play until written clearance by a licensed provider
a SafeSport course for the athlete
test.why: Washington's law required removal and written clearance from a licensed health care provider.

test.q: Which rule maker, founded in Chicago in 1920, writes high school wrestling rules?
test.why: The NFHS writes national high school rule books, including weight management and skin checks.

test.q: What did the Amateur Sports Act of 1978 do for sports like judo and taekwondo?
choices: It let the U.S. Olympic Committee recognize one national governing body for each sport.
It moved them into PE classes.
test.why: The 1978 law set up one national governing body per Olympic sport, such as USA Judo and USA Taekwondo.

write.prompt: Who should be most responsible for safety in a combat sport: the state, a national governing body or the school? Cite at least three dated records from this unit, such as the Walker Law (1920), the Lystedt Law (2009), the Amateur Sports Act (1978) or the Illinois Tort Immunity Act (1965).
tips: Name each law or record and give its year.
Say what each record required and who had to follow it.
Compare two rule makers fairly before you choose one.
Use unit words such as athletic commission, national governing body and negligence.
